a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: L1 human absolute-bioavailability records for ester-containing or basic-amine drugs are above the 20% threshold: benazepril 28–37% (C01, C16), pivampicillin 50–89% (C03, C13, C21), tamoxifen approximately 100% (C02, C04, C05), norethisterone 47–73% (C11), and encainide 76–78% in cirrhosis (C08, C12, C19). This indicates that the query's acetate ester and tertiary amine do not by themselves support F < 20%.

L4 absorption/permeability evidence for basic lipophilic amines supports adequate absorption despite the query's low neutral fraction: imipramine is essentially 100% absorbed in humans (C52, C56, C61), diphenhydramine, chlorpromazine, and promethazine show high Caco-2 absorptive permeability (C60, C62, C53, C55, C57), and nabumetone is reported well absorbed after oral administration (C59).

L5 gut-wall efflux/intestinal-metabolism records do not provide affirmative low-F evidence: promethazine shows passive, non-directional transport with no significant efflux (C65, C67, C73), imipramine shows high Caco-2 permeability consistent with 100% absorption (C74), compound 16a shows high A→B permeability with an efflux ratio of 0.7 (C63, C66), and CBL0174 shows a modest B→A/A→B ratio of about 1.2 (C69, C72). Tamoxifen is identified as a P-gp substrate yet has approximately 100% human oral bioavailability (C64 with C02/C04/C05), so efflux substrate status alone is not evidence for F < 20%.

The apixaban rifampin context (C10, C15, C18, C31, C33) and its Caco-2 efflux record (C51) are not transferable low-F evidence for the query: apixaban absolute oral bioavailability was 37–39% even under strong CYP3A4/P-gp induction, and the query is a different, more lipophilic basic molecule.

The modified-release condition affects release rate and exposure profile, but no supplied record shows that modified release reduces the extent of absorption below the 20% absolute-bioavailability threshold for this molecule class.
